title: Τειρεσίου θέσφατα
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus, still telling his story, hears the rest of what the seer Tiresias has to say beside the pit of blood. Poseidon, angry for his blinded son, will make the homecoming hard; if Odysseus and his men leave the cattle of the Sun unharmed on the island of Thrinacia they may still reach Ithaca, and if not he will come home late, alone and in another man’s ship, to find the suitors devouring his house. After he has punished them he must carry an oar inland until a traveller takes it for a winnowing-shovel, plant it, sacrifice to Poseidon, and go home; death will come to him from the sea, a mild death, in a sleek old age with his people prosperous about him. Tiresias goes back into Hades, and Odysseus’s mother, who has drunk the blood, knows him at once. She asks how he came living to this place, and he asks how she died and what is happening at home. She tells of his wife’s tears, of his father sleeping in the dust beside the fire, and of her own death, which came from longing for him. Three times he tries to take hold of her, and three times her shade slips from his hands like a dream.

sentences.t: νόστον δίζηαι μελιηδέα, φαίδιμ’ Ὀδυσσεῦ·
sentences.tr: noston dizēai meliēdea, phaidim’ Odysseu·
sentences.l: ‘A homecoming you seek, honey-sweet, glorious Odysseus;
sentences.i: ‘You are seeking a honey-sweet homecoming, glorious Odysseus;
sentences.n: Tiresias speaks, and his speech runs on to line 137. νόστον is ‘homecoming’, the poem’s great theme, and δίζηαι is ‘you seek’, the 2nd sg. of δίζημαι. μελιηδέα ‘honey-sweet’ is a stock epithet. φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ is another, here in the vocative; it is translated the same way every time, even where it sits oddly, as it will at 128 beside a shoulder.

sentences.t: τὸν δέ τοι ἀργαλέον θήσει θεός·
sentences.tr: ton de toi argaleon thēsei theos·
sentences.l: and it for you grievous will make a god;
sentences.i: but a god will make it grievous for you;
sentences.n: τὸν is ‘it’, the homecoming of the line before: in Homer the old demonstrative that later became the article is a pronoun. ἀργαλέον ‘grievous’ is the complement of θήσει, the future of τίθημι ‘make’. τοι is Homer’s form of σοι ‘to you, for you’. The god is not named yet; the next unit names him by an epithet.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ὀίω
λήσειν ἐννοσίγαιον, ὅ τοι κότον ἔνθετο θυμῷ
χωόμενος ὅτι οἱ υἱὸν φίλον ἐξαλάωσας.
sentences.tr:
ou gar oiō
lēsein ennosigaion, ho toi koton entheto thymōi
chōomenos hoti hoi huion philon exalaōsas.
sentences.i: for I do not think you will escape the earth-shaker, who has set resentment in his heart against you, angry because you blinded his dear son.
sentences.n: ὀίω ‘I think’ governs the future infinitive λήσειν, ‘that you will escape the notice of’, with ἐννοσίγαιον ‘earth-shaker’ in the accusative, a name for Poseidon built on γαῖα ‘earth’. ὅ τοι is ‘who … against you’ (ὅ the old demonstrative, here used as a relative; τοι = σοι). κότον ἔνθετο θυμῷ is ‘put resentment in his heart’: ἔνθετο is an unaugmented aorist middle of ἐντίθημι. οἱ is ‘his’, the dative of the owner; the son is not named. ἐξαλάωσας is from ἐξαλαόω, ‘blind completely’, from ἀλαός ‘blind’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἔτι μέν κε καὶ ὣς κακά περ πάσχοντες ἵκοισθε,
αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃς σὸν θυμὸν ἐρυκακέειν καὶ ἑταίρων,
sentences.tr:
all’ eti men ke kai hōs kaka per paschontes hikoisthe,
ai k’ ethelēis son thymon erykakeein kai hetairōn,
sentences.l:
But still, even so, evils though suffering, you might arrive,
if you are willing to hold back your heart and your companions’,
sentences.i: Even so you may still arrive, though you suffer hardships, if you are willing to hold back your heart and those of your companions,
sentences.n: κε with the optative ἵκοισθε is ‘you might arrive’; πάσχοντες is plural, so Tiresias is speaking of Odysseus and his men together. καὶ ὥς is ‘even so’, with ὥς the adverb. αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃς is αἰ κε + subjunctive, ‘if you are willing’, Attic ἐὰν ἐθέλῃς. ἐρυκακέειν is the reduplicated aorist infinitive of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’, an epic form. σὸν θυμὸν … καὶ ἑταίρων is ‘your heart and (the hearts) of your companions’. The unit stops at a comma because the whole sentence would run past four lines.

sentences.t:
ὁππότε κε πρῶτον πελάσῃς ἐυεργέα νῆα
Θρινακίῃ νήσῳ, προφυγὼν ἰοειδέα πόντον,
βοσκομένας δ’ εὕρητε βόας καὶ ἴφια μῆλα
Ἠελίου, ὃς πάντ’ ἐφορᾷ καὶ πάντ’ ἐπακούει.
sentences.tr:
hoppote ke prōton pelasēis eyergea nēa
Thrinakiēi nēsōi, prophygōn ioeidea ponton,
boskomenas d’ heurēte boas kai iphia mēla
Ēeliou, hos pant’ ephorāi kai pant’ epakouei.
sentences.l:
whenever first you bring near your well-made ship
to the island Thrinacia, having escaped the violet-dark sea,
and find grazing the cattle and the stout flocks
of the Sun, who oversees all things and listens to all things.
sentences.i: When you first bring your well-made ship to the island of Thrinacia, having escaped the violet-dark sea, you will find the cattle and the stout flocks of the Sun grazing there, the Sun who sees everything and hears everything.
sentences.n: ὁππότε κε πρῶτον πελάσῃς is ‘whenever first you bring near’, with κε and the subjunctive; the verb shifts to the plural at εὕρητε, ‘you (all) find’. Θρινακίῃ νήσῳ is the dative of the goal after πελάσῃς, ‘to the island Thrinacia’; Θρινακίῃ is an adjective, ‘Thrinacian’, in -ῃ where Attic has -ᾳ. ἐυεργέα ‘well-made’ and ἰοειδέα ‘violet-dark’ are stock words (ἴον ‘violet’ + εἶδος). ἴφια, of the flocks, is ‘stout’ (the traditional gloss); μῆλα are small livestock, sheep and goats together. Ἠελίου is the Sun, Attic Ἡλίου. ἐφορᾷ and ἐπακούει are ‘oversees’ and ‘listens to’: nothing escapes him.

sentences.t:
τὰς εἰ μέν κ’ ἀσινέας ἐάᾳς νόστου τε μέδηαι,
καί κεν ἔτ’ εἰς Ἰθάκην κακά περ πάσχοντες ἵκοισθε·
sentences.tr:
tas ei men k’ asineas eaāis nostou te medēai,
kai ken et’ eis Ithakēn kaka per paschontes hikoisthe·
sentences.l:
Them, if you leave unharmed and are mindful of the homecoming,
then too you might still reach Ithaca, evils though suffering;
sentences.i: If you leave them unharmed and keep your mind on getting home, you may still reach Ithaca, though you suffer hardships;
sentences.n: τὰς, ‘them’, is feminine plural and picks up the cattle (βόας); the flocks go with them in the sense. ἀσινέας is ‘unharmed’; ἐάᾳς is the present subjunctive of ἐάω ‘leave alone, allow’, with the vowels left open (Attic ἐᾷς). νόστου τε μέδηαι is ‘and are mindful of homecoming’: μέδομαι takes the genitive. The apodosis καί κεν ἔτ’ … ἵκοισθε echoes line 104 (κακά περ πάσχοντες ἵκοισθε recurs), and that echo is the point: the same outcome is offered again.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κε σίνηαι, τότε τοι τεκμαίρομ’ ὄλεθρον,
νηί τε καὶ ἑτάροις.
sentences.tr:
ei de ke sinēai, tote toi tekmairom’ olethron,
nēi te kai hetarois.
sentences.l:
but if you harm them, then for you I fix destruction,
for ship and companions;
sentences.i: But if you do them harm, then I fix destruction for you, for your ship and your companions;
sentences.n: σίνηαι is the subjunctive of σίνομαι ‘harm, plunder’. τεκμαίρομαι is ‘I fix’, ‘I mark out’: the seer declares what is decreed. The full stop falls in the middle of line 113, so the unit ends there and the rest of the line opens the next. ἑτάροις is the same word as ἑταίροις; the poet uses whichever form suits the line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ εἴ πέρ κεν ἀλύξῃς,
ὀψὲ κακῶς νεῖαι, ὀλέσας ἄπο πάντας ἑταίρους,
νηὸς ἐπ’ ἀλλοτρίης·
sentences.tr:
autos d’ ei per ken alyxēis,
opse kakōs neiai, olesas apo pantas hetairous,
nēos ep’ allotriēs·
sentences.i: But you yourself, even if you escape, will come home late and in misery, having lost all your companions, on a ship not your own;
sentences.n: αὐτὸς δ’ opens a contrast: ‘you yourself’, as against the ship and men. εἴ πέρ κεν ἀλύξῃς is ‘even if you escape’; νεῖαι is ‘you will come’ (from νέομαι, the verb of coming home); ὀλέσας ἄπο is tmesis, ἀπολέσας ‘having lost’. ἀλλοτρίης is ‘belonging to another’. The unit begins in the middle of line 113 and ends in the middle of line 115, at the high dot.

sentences.t:
δήεις δ’ ἐν πήματα οἴκῳ,
ἄνδρας ὑπερφιάλους, οἵ τοι βίοτον κατέδουσι
μνώμενοι ἀντιθέην ἄλοχον καὶ ἕδνα διδόντες.
sentences.tr:
dēeis d’ en pēmata oikōi,
andras hyperphialous, hoi toi bioton katedousi
mnōmenoi antitheēn alochon kai hedna didontes.
sentences.l:
and you will find woes in your house,
men overweening, who eat up your livelihood,
wooing your godlike wife and bridal gifts giving.
sentences.i: and you will find woes in your house: overweening men, who are eating up your livelihood while they woo your godlike wife and offer her bridal gifts.
sentences.n: δήεις is ‘you will find’, a future of an old verb. ἐν … οἴκῳ is ‘in the house’: the preposition stands apart from its noun, with πήματα ‘woes’ between (word order, not tmesis, which parts a preverb from its verb). ἄνδρας ὑπερφιάλους is in apposition to the woes. ὑπερφίαλος is ‘overweening’. οἵ τοι is ‘who, to your cost’. βίοτον is ‘livelihood’, and κατέδουσι ‘eat down, devour’. ἀντιθέην is the feminine accusative of ἀντίθεος ‘godlike’; ἕδνα, here without the usual extra ε, are ‘bridal gifts’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι κείνων γε βίας ἀποτίσεαι ἐλθών·
sentences.tr: all’ ē toi keinōn ge bias apotiseai elthōn·
sentences.l: But truly their violent deeds you will exact payment for, having come;
sentences.i: But you will indeed exact payment from them for their violence when you come.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι is ‘but truly’. κείνων is ‘of those men’ (Attic ἐκείνων). βίας is the accusative plural of βία (Ionic βίη), ‘acts of violence’. ἀποτίσεαι is the future middle of ἀποτίνω, with the uncontracted ending -εαι (Attic -ῃ): to take payment for a wrong for oneself, to avenge. ἐλθών is ‘once you have come’, that is, home to Ithaca.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν μνηστῆρας ἐνὶ μεγάροισι τεοῖσι
κτείνῃς ἠὲ δόλῳ ἢ ἀμφαδὸν ὀξέι χαλκῷ,
ἔρχεσθαι δὴ ἔπειτα λαβὼν ἐυῆρες ἐρετμόν,
sentences.tr:
autar epēn mnēstēras eni megaroisi teoisi
kteinēis ēe dolōi ē amphadon oxei chalkōi,
erchesthai dē epeita labōn eyēres eretmon,
sentences.l:
And when the suitors in your halls
you have killed, either by guile or openly with the sharp bronze,
to go then indeed, taking a well-fitted oar,
sentences.i: And when you have killed the suitors in your halls, whether by guile or in the open with the sharp bronze, then take a well-fitted oar and go,
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπήν is ‘but when’ (ἐπήν = ἐπεὶ ἄν); with κτείνῃς, the subjunctive, it is ‘when you have killed’. The two ways, δόλῳ ‘by guile’ and ἀμφαδόν ‘openly’, are a pair. ὀξέι χαλκῷ is ‘with the sharp bronze’, a dative in -ι, Attic ὀξεῖ. ἔρχεσθαι is an infinitive used as a command, ‘to go!’. ἐυῆρες is ‘well-fitted’, a compound that comes from ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’. The unit stops at a comma, because the sentence runs on for several lines.

sentences.t:
εἰς ὅ κε τοὺς ἀφίκηαι οἳ οὐκ ἴσασι θάλασσαν
ἀνέρες, οὐδέ θ’ ἅλεσσι μεμιγμένον εἶδαρ ἔδουσιν·
sentences.tr:
eis ho ke tous aphikēai hoi ouk isasi thalassan
aneres, oude th’ halessi memigmenon eidar edousin·
sentences.l:
until you reach those who do not know the sea,
men who not even food mixed with salt eat;
sentences.i: until you come to men who know nothing of the sea and eat no food mixed with salt;
sentences.n: εἰς ὅ κε … ἀφίκηαι is ‘until you reach’: κε with the subjunctive. οἳ οὐκ ἴσασι is ‘who do not know’, ἴσασι being a form of οἶδα. ἀνέρες ‘men’, with its first syllable lengthened for the metre, is nominative and stands in apposition to the relative οἳ: ‘those who …, men who …’. ἅλεσσι is a dative plural of ἅλς ‘salt’ (the same word is ‘sea’ in the feminine), and εἶδαρ is a rare word for ‘food’. Men who eat unsalted food live far from the sea, and so have never seen an oar.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα τοί γ’ ἴσασι νέας φοινικοπαρῄους
οὐδ’ ἐυήρε’ ἐρετμά, τά τε πτερὰ νηυσὶ πέλονται.
sentences.tr:
oud’ ara toi g’ isasi neas phoinikoparēious
oud’ eyēre’ eretma, ta te ptera nēusi pelontai.
sentences.l:
nor indeed do they know ships crimson-cheeked,
nor well-fitted oars, which wings for ships are.
sentences.i: nor do they know ships with crimson cheeks, or well-fitted oars, which serve ships as wings.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἄρα τοί γ’ is ‘nor indeed do they’. φοινικοπαρῄους is ‘crimson-cheeked’: the ‘cheeks’ are the sides of the bow, painted red. ἐυήρε’ is ἐυήρεα, the neuter plural of the adjective met at 121. τά τε is ‘which’, with the epic τε that marks a general truth. πτερά is ‘wings’, and the oars are called wings of the ship; compare the winged words that fly from a speaker.

sentences.t: σῆμα δέ τοι ἐρέω μάλ’ ἀριφραδές, οὐδέ σε λήσει·
sentences.tr: sēma de toi ereō mal’ ariphrades, oude se lēsei·
sentences.l: And a sign to you I will tell, very plain, and it will not escape you:
sentences.i: And I will tell you a sign, very plain, that will not escape you:
sentences.n: σῆμα is ‘sign’, the token by which Odysseus will know the place. ἐρέω is ‘I will tell’, a future of the verb of speaking. ἀριφραδές is ‘very plain’: ἀρι- is an intensifying prefix, and the rest is from φράζω ‘show, make clear’; μάλ’ adds a second ‘very’, which English gives only once. οὐδέ σε λήσει is ‘and it will not escape you’, a negative that reinforces the positive.

sentences.t:
ὁππότε κεν δή τοι συμβλήμενος ἄλλος ὁδίτης
φήῃ ἀθηρηλοιγὸν ἔχειν ἀνὰ φαιδίμῳ ὤμῳ,
sentences.tr:
hoppote ken dē toi symblēmenos allos hoditēs
phēēi athērēloigon echein ana phaidimōi ōmōi,
sentences.l:
Whenever indeed, meeting you, another wayfarer
shall say a chaff-ruiner you have on your glorious shoulder,
sentences.i: When another traveller meets you and says that you are carrying a winnowing-shovel on your glorious shoulder,
sentences.n: συμβλήμενος is the aorist middle participle of συμβάλλω, ‘meeting’, here with the dative τοι. φήῃ is the present subjunctive of φημί (Attic φῇ), ‘shall say’, and ἀνά with the dative is ‘upon’. ἀθηρηλοιγόν is ‘a chaff-ruiner’: a winnowing-shovel is the ancient explanation, and the first half of the word is disputed (the awn or the husk of grain). φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ is here applied to a shoulder, because the epithet is translated the same way every time. A man who takes an oar for a grain-shovel has never seen the sea.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότε δὴ γαίῃ πήξας ἐυῆρες ἐρετμόν,
ῥέξας ἱερὰ καλὰ Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι,
ἀρνειὸν ταῦρόν τε συῶν τ’ ἐπιβήτορα κάπρον,
sentences.tr:
kai tote dē gaiēi pēxas eyēres eretmon,
rhexas hiera kala Poseidaōni anakti,
arneion tauron te syōn t’ epibētora kapron,
sentences.l:
and then indeed in the earth fixing the well-fitted oar,
and offering fine sacrifices to Poseidon the lord,
a ram and a bull and a boar, mounter of sows,
sentences.i: then fix the well-fitted oar in the ground and make fine sacrifices to lord Poseidon: a ram, a bull, and a boar that mounts sows,
sentences.n: καὶ τότε δή is ‘and then indeed’. γαίῃ, a dative, is ‘in the earth’, and πήξας ‘having fixed’ is from πήγνυμι. ῥέξας is ‘having offered’, from ῥέζω; ἱερά are ‘sacrifices’. Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι is ‘to Poseidon the lord’, the god he has wronged. The three animals are ἀρνειόν ‘a ram’, ταῦρον ‘a bull’ and κάπρον ‘a boar’; ἐπιβήτορα, ‘mounter’, says that the boar is a breeder, and συῶν is ‘of swine’, here sows. The command ‘go home’, which these participles lead up to, comes in the next unit.

sentences.t:
οἴκαδ’ ἀποστείχειν ἔρδειν θ’ ἱερᾶς ἑκατόμβας
ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι, τοὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσι,
πᾶσι μάλ’ ἑξείης.
sentences.tr:
oikad’ aposteichein erdein th’ hieras hekatombas
athanatoisi theoisi, toi ouranon euryn echousi,
pasi mal’ hexeiēs.
sentences.l:
to go off home, and to offer sacred hecatombs
to the immortal gods, who hold the wide sky,
to all, quite in order, one after another.
sentences.i: Then go back home and offer sacred hecatombs to the immortal gods who hold the broad heaven, to every one of them in turn.
sentences.n: οἴκαδ’ is ‘homeward’, with -δε of direction. ἀποστείχειν and ἔρδειν are both infinitives used as commands, like ἔρχεσθαι at 121. ἱερᾶς ἑκατόμβας, ‘sacred hecatombs’, and the half-line ‘to the immortal gods, who hold the wide sky’ are formulas, and they keep the English already given them in an earlier part. ἑξείης is ‘in order, one after another’, strengthened by μάλ’. The full stop falls in the middle of line 134.

sentences.t:
θάνατος δέ τοι ἐξ ἁλὸς αὐτῷ
ἀβληχρὸς μάλα τοῖος ἐλεύσεται, ὅς κέ σε πέφνῃ
γήραι ὕπο λιπαρῷ ἀρημένον·
sentences.tr:
thanatos de toi ex halos autōi
ablēchros mala toios eleusetai, hos ke se pephnēi
gērai hypo liparōi arēmenon·
sentences.i: And death will come to you from the sea, a very mild death, such as will kill you when you are worn out under a sleek old age;
sentences.n: ἐξ ἁλός is ‘from the sea’, and it can also mean ‘away from the sea’; the Greek leaves the question open and the English keeps the plain ‘from’. ἀβληχρός is ‘mild’: its exact meaning is not known (‘gentle’, ‘feeble’, and ‘slow’ have all been guessed). τοῖος … ὅς κε is ‘of the kind that’, and πέφνῃ is the aorist subjunctive of an old verb ‘slay’. γήραι is the dative of γῆρας ‘old age’; λιπαρῷ, ‘sleek’, is from λίπα ‘oil’, hence ‘glossy, prosperous’. ἀρημένον ‘worn down’ agrees with σε. The unit begins in the middle of line 134.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δὲ λαοὶ
ὄλβιοι ἔσσονται.
sentences.tr:
amphi de laoi
olbioi essontai.
sentences.l:
and around you the peoples
prosperous will be.
sentences.i: and all about you the people will be prosperous.
sentences.n: ἀμφί here is an adverb, ‘around, about you’. λαοί are ‘the peoples’, the folk of the country. ὄλβιοι is ‘prosperous’; ἔσσονται is the future of εἰμί with the doubled σ of the epic. The full stop falls in the middle of line 137.

sentences.t: τὰ δέ τοι νημερτέα εἴρω.
sentences.tr: ta de toi nēmertea eirō.
sentences.l: And these things to you unerring I tell.’
sentences.i: What I tell you is unerring.’
sentences.n: τὰ is a pronoun, ‘these things’ (so too τὰ μέν at 139). νημερτέα is ‘unerring’, said of the prophecy. εἴρω is ‘I tell’, a present formed from the root of ἐρέω. Tiresias’s speech ends here, and the quotation mark closes.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ μιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, autar egō min ameibomenos proseeipon·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and I then, answering her, addressed her:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is ‘so (he) spoke’: ἔφατ’ is ἔφατο, elided, the augmented imperfect of φημί. The Greek does not mark the speaker’s sex, and the speaker here is Tiresias, so the English ‘she’ is wrong for this line. It is the wording already fixed in an earlier part for the same Greek, where the speaker was a woman, and a repeated line must keep its published English; read it as ‘So he spoke, and I answered him and said.’ ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον is ‘answering, I addressed’. Odysseus is still the narrator, so the quotation marks stop at the end of the unit before and begin again at his own words.

sentences.t: Τειρεσίη, τὰ μὲν ἄρ που ἐπέκλωσαν θεοὶ αὐτοί.
sentences.tr: Teiresiē, ta men ar pou epeklōsan theoi autoi.
sentences.l: ‘Tiresias, these things, I suppose, the gods themselves have spun.
sentences.i: ‘Tiresias, these things, I suppose, the gods themselves have spun for me.
sentences.n: Τειρεσίη is the vocative of Τειρεσίας, with Ionic -η where Attic would have -α. ἐπέκλωσαν is the aorist of ἐπικλώθω ‘spin to’, with the augment between preverb and stem: the gods spin a thread for a man, and what is spun cannot be undone. ἄρ που is ‘I suppose’, a mild, resigned particle pair. θεοὶ αὐτοί is ‘the gods themselves’; the pronoun of the person affected is left to be understood.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον·
sentences.tr: all’ age moi tode eipe kai atrekeōs katalexon·
sentences.l: But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly;
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, and set it out for me exactly:
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, a stock opening to a request, followed by two imperatives, εἰπέ and κατάλεξον (the aorist imperative of καταλέγω ‘recount’). μοι is ‘to me’. ἀτρεκέως is ‘exactly’. The whole line is a formula, and it has the English it already has in an earlier part.

sentences.t: μητρὸς τήνδ’ ὁρόω ψυχὴν κατατεθνηυίης·
sentences.tr: mētros tēnd’ horoō psychēn katatethnēuiēs·
sentences.l: Of my mother this soul I see, of her who has died;
sentences.i: I see here the soul of my mother, who has died;
sentences.n: ὁρόω is the uncontracted ‘I see’ (Attic ὁρῶ). μητρὸς … ψυχήν is ‘the soul of my mother’, with the genitive placed first for emphasis, and τήνδ’ ‘this’ points to her. κατατεθνηυίης is the genitive feminine of the perfect participle of καταθνῄσκω, ‘who has died’; the form is Homeric, with -υίης where Attic would have -υίας. ψυχή is translated ‘soul’ in this part.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἀκέουσ’ ἧσται σχεδὸν αἵματος, οὐδ’ ἑὸν υἱὸν
ἔτλη ἐσάντα ἰδεῖν οὐδὲ προτιμυθήσασθαι.
sentences.tr:
hē d’ akeous’ hēstai schedon haimatos, oud’ heon huion
etlē esanta idein oude protimythēsasthai.
sentences.l:
and she, in silence, sits near the blood, nor her own son
has endured to look at face to face, nor to speak to.
sentences.i: She sits in silence near the blood, and cannot bring herself to look her own son in the face or to speak to him.
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ is ‘and she’, the article as a pronoun. ἀκέουσα is ‘in silence’, the feminine of ἀκέων ‘silent’. ἧσται is ‘sits’. ἑὸν is the possessive ‘her own’, not a relative. ἔτλη, the aorist of τλάω, is ‘had the heart, brought herself’; the infinitives ἰδεῖν and προτιμυθήσασθαι are ‘to look at’ and ‘to speak to’. ἐσάντα is ‘face to face’. She does not speak until she has drunk the blood (152–154).

sentences.t: εἰπέ, ἄναξ, πῶς κέν με ἀναγνοίη τὸν ἐόντα;
sentences.tr: eipe, anax, pōs ken me anagnoiē ton eonta;
sentences.l: Tell, lord, how might she know me, being the one I am?’
sentences.i: Tell me, lord, how might she recognize me for who I am?’
sentences.n: ἄναξ is ‘lord’, the address to Tiresias. πῶς κεν … ἀναγνοίη is the potential optative, ‘how might she recognize’, from ἀναγιγνώσκω. τὸν ἐόντα is literally ‘me, the one being (so)’: a living man, not a shade. The question is the practical one, how a ghost can know a living son; Tiresias answers at once. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δέ μ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν·
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, ho de m’ autik’ ameibomenos proseeipen·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and he then at once, answering me, addressed me:
sentences.i: So I said, and he answered me at once:
sentences.n: ὣς ἐφάμην is ‘so I spoke’, the middle imperfect of φημί. The line is a reply-formula, and its English is the wording already fixed for it. ὁ, the old demonstrative, is ‘he’; μ’ is ‘me’; αὐτίκα is ‘at once’. The speaker is again Tiresias.

sentences.t: ῥηΐδιόν τοι ἔπος ἐρέω καὶ ἐπὶ φρεσὶ θήσω.
sentences.tr: rhēïdion toi epos ereō kai epi phresi thēsō.
sentences.l: ‘An easy word to you I will say, and in your mind I will place it.
sentences.i: ‘I will tell you an easy thing, and set it in your mind.
sentences.n: ῥηΐδιον is ‘easy’ (Attic ῥᾴδιον), agreeing with ἔπος ‘word’, the object of ἐρέω. ἐρέω is ‘I will say’. ἐπὶ φρεσὶ θήσω is ‘I will set it upon your mind’, a promise that the answer will be plain and will stay with him; φρεσί, the dative plural of φρήν, is ‘mind’. τοι is ‘to you’.

sentences.t:
ὅν τινα μέν κεν ἐᾷς νεκύων κατατεθνηώτων
αἵματος ἆσσον ἴμεν, ὁ δέ τοι νημερτὲς ἐνίψει·
sentences.tr:
hon tina men ken eāis nekyōn katatethnēōtōn
haimatos asson imen, ho de toi nēmertes enipsei·
sentences.l:
Whomever of the dead, of those who have died, you allow
nearer the blood to go, he will tell you what is unerring;
sentences.i: Any one of the dead, of those who have died, whom you allow to come nearer the blood will tell you what is unerring;
sentences.n: ὅν τινα … ἐᾷς is ‘whichever one you allow’, with the object of the verb before it. ἐᾷς is the subjunctive of ἐάω, with κεν (‘whichever, in case’). νεκύων κατατεθνηώτων is ‘of the dead, of those who have died’; the perfect participle repeats the idea of the noun. αἵματος ἆσσον ἴμεν is ‘to go nearer the blood’, with ἴμεν the epic infinitive of εἶμι; ἆσσον, the comparative of ἄγχι, takes the genitive. νημερτές, ‘unerring’, is neuter, ‘what is unerring’ (it could also be read as an adverb, ‘unerringly’), and ἐνίψει is the future of ἐνίπτω ‘tell’.

sentences.t: ᾧ δέ κ’ ἐπιφθονέῃς, ὁ δέ τοι πάλιν εἶσιν ὀπίσσω.
sentences.tr: hōi de k’ epiphthoneēis, ho de toi palin eisin opissō.
sentences.l: and to whom you grudge it, he will go back again, behind.’
sentences.i: but anyone to whom you begrudge it will go back again.’
sentences.n: ᾧ δέ κ’ ἐπιφθονέῃς is ‘and to whom you begrudge (it)’, the counterpart of the last unit’s relative clause; ἐπιφθονέω means ‘grudge’ with the dative. The thing begrudged, the blood, is understood. πάλιν … ὀπίσσω is a doubled adverb, ‘back again’. εἶσιν is the present of εἶμι ‘go’, with future sense. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φαμένη ψυχὴ μὲν ἔβη δόμον Ἄϊδος εἴσω
Τειρεσίαο ἄνακτος, ἐπεὶ κατὰ θέσφατ’ ἔλεξεν·
sentences.tr:
hōs phamenē psychē men ebē domon Aïdos eisō
Teiresiao anaktos, epei kata thesphat’ elexen·
sentences.l:
So saying, the soul the house of Hades went into,
of lord Tiresias, when the prophecies he had recounted;
sentences.i: So speaking, the soul of lord Tiresias went into the house of Hades, when he had recounted his prophecies;
sentences.n: ὣς φαμένη is ‘so speaking’, in the feminine, because it agrees with ψυχή ‘soul’; the soul of a man is grammatically feminine, whatever the man was. ψυχὴ μὲν ἔβη is ‘the soul went’, with ἔβη the aorist of βαίνω. δόμον Ἄϊδος εἴσω is ‘into the house of Hades’. Τειρεσίαο ἄνακτος is ‘of lord Tiresias’, a genitive in -αο (Attic -ου). κατὰ … ἔλεξεν is tmesis for κατέλεξεν ‘had recounted’; θέσφατα are ‘prophecies’, what the gods have declared.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν αὐτοῦ μένον ἔμπεδον, ὄφρ’ ἐπὶ μήτηρ
ἤλυθε καὶ πίεν αἷμα κελαινεφές·
sentences.tr:
autar egōn autou menon empedon, ophr’ epi mētēr
ēlythe kai pien haima kelainephes·
sentences.l:
but I in that very place stayed steadily, until my mother
came up and drank the dark-clouded blood;
sentences.i: But I stayed right there, steadily, until my mother came up and drank the blood dark as a cloud;
sentences.n: αὐτοῦ is ‘in that very place’. ἔμπεδον is ‘steadily, without a break’. ὄφρ’ … ἤλυθε is ‘until … came’; ἐπὶ … ἤλυθε is tmesis, ἐπήλυθε ‘came up’, and ἤλυθε is the epic form of the aorist ἦλθε. πίεν is the unaugmented aorist of πίνω. κελαινεφές is ‘dark-clouded’ (κελαινός ‘dark’ + νέφος ‘cloud’), here said of the blood. The unit ends at the high dot in the middle of line 153.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ ἔγνω,
καί μ’ ὀλοφυρομένη ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
autika d’ egnō,
kai m’ olophyromenē epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
and at once she knew me,
and to me, lamenting, winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: and at once she knew me, and, lamenting, spoke winged words to me:
sentences.n: αὐτίκα δ’ ἔγνω is ‘and at once she knew (me)’, with ἔγνω the aorist of γιγνώσκω; the mother knows her son as soon as she has drunk. ὀλοφυρομένη is ‘lamenting’. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the standing phrase for a speech, ‘winged words’, and is given the same English every time. The second line already stands in an earlier part and keeps its wording.

sentences.t:
τέκνον ἐμόν, πῶς ἦλθες ὑπὸ ζόφον ἠερόεντα
ζωὸς ἐών;
sentences.tr:
teknon emon, pōs ēlthes hypo zophon ēeroenta
zōos eōn;
sentences.l:
‘My child, how did you come beneath the misty gloom,
being alive?
sentences.i: ‘My child, how did you come beneath the misty gloom, while still alive?
sentences.n: This is Odysseus’s mother speaking; in this part she is called only ‘mother’. τέκνον ἐμόν is ‘my child’. ὑπὸ ζόφον ἠερόεντα is ‘beneath the misty gloom’, the dark of Hades, ζόφος being the dark of the west, ἠερόεντα ‘misty’ from ἀήρ. ζωὸς ἐών is ‘being alive’, with ἐών the Ionic participle of εἰμί.

sentences.t: χαλεπὸν δὲ τάδε ζωοῖσιν ὁρᾶσθαι.
sentences.tr: chalepon de tade zōoisin horasthai.
sentences.l: And hard these things for the living to behold.
sentences.i: These things are hard for the living to look upon.
sentences.n: χαλεπόν is ‘hard’, said of a task, and ζωοῖσιν is a dative plural in -οισιν, ‘for the living’. ὁρᾶσθαι is the infinitive ‘to be seen’, or ‘to look upon’: the construction can be read either way, and the sense is the same. τάδε points to the place and its sights.

sentences.t:
μέσσῳ γὰρ μεγάλοι ποταμοὶ καὶ δεινὰ ῥέεθρα,
Ὠκεανὸς μὲν πρῶτα, τὸν οὔ πως ἔστι περῆσαι
πεζὸν ἐόντ’, ἢν μή τις ἔχῃ ἐυεργέα νῆα.
sentences.tr:
messōi gar megaloi potamoi kai deina rheethra,
Ōkeanos men prōta, ton ou pōs esti perēsai
pezon eont’, ēn mē tis echēi eyergea nēa.
sentences.l:
For in between are great rivers and dread streams,
Oceanus first, which in no way is it possible to cross
being on foot, unless someone have a well-made ship.
sentences.i: For between lie great rivers and dread streams, and first of all Oceanus, which no one can cross on foot, unless he has a well-made ship.
sentences.n: μέσσῳ is ‘in the middle, between’ (the doubled σ is the epic form of μέσῳ). δεινά is ‘dread’, ῥέεθρα ‘streams’. Ὠκεανὸς μὲν πρῶτα is ‘Oceanus, to begin with’. τὸν οὔ πως ἔστι περῆσαι is ‘which in no way is it possible to cross’, with ἔστι ‘it is possible’ and an aorist infinitive. πεζὸν ἐόντ’ is ‘being on foot’. ἢν μή τις ἔχῃ is ‘unless anyone has’, ἤν for ἐάν. ἐυεργέα ‘well-made’ describes the ship as it did at 106.

sentences.t:
ἦ νῦν δὴ Τροίηθεν ἀλώμενος ἐνθάδ’ ἱκάνεις
νηί τε καὶ ἑτάροισι πολὺν χρόνον;
sentences.tr:
ē nyn dē Troiēthen alōmenos enthad’ hikaneis
nēi te kai hetaroisi polyn chronon;
sentences.l:
Is it, then, only now, from Troy wandering, that you come here
with ship and companions, a long time?
sentences.i: Is it only now, after wandering from Troy a long time with your ship and your companions, that you have come here?
sentences.n: ἦ is the sign of a question, here with νῦν δή ‘only now’. Τροίηθεν is ‘from Troy’, with the suffix -θεν of place from which, and Τροίη with Ionic η. ἀλώμενος ἐνθάδ’ ἱκάνεις is ‘wandering you come here’. νηί τε καὶ ἑτάροισι is ‘with ship and companions’, a dative of accompaniment in -οισι. πολὺν χρόνον is an accusative of time, ‘for a long time’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ πω ἦλθες
εἰς Ἰθάκην, οὐδ’ εἶδες ἐνὶ μεγάροισι γυναῖκα;
sentences.tr:
oude pō ēlthes
eis Ithakēn, oud’ eides eni megaroisi gynaika;
sentences.l:
and not yet have you come
to Ithaca, nor seen in the halls your wife?’
sentences.i: And have you not yet come to Ithaca, or seen your wife in your halls?’
sentences.n: The first question ends at the Greek question mark in the middle of line 161, and this unit begins there. οὐδέ πω ἦλθες is ‘and have you not yet come’. εἰς Ἰθάκην is ‘to Ithaca’, and the second οὐδ’ εἶδες adds ‘nor seen’. ἐνὶ μεγάροισι is ‘in the halls’, and γυναῖκα, ‘wife’, is without a possessive, as often in Greek. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ μιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, autar egō min ameibomenos proseeipon·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and I then, answering her, addressed her:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
sentences.n: This is the same formula as at 138, and it has the same English. The speaker is now Odysseus’s mother, so the English ‘she’ is right here. ἔφατ’ is ἔφατο, elided, the augmented imperfect of φημί; ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον is ‘answering, I addressed’.

sentences.t:
μῆτερ ἐμή, χρειώ με κατήγαγεν εἰς Ἀίδαο
ψυχῇ χρησόμενον Θηβαίου Τειρεσίαο·
sentences.tr:
mēter emē, chreiō me katēgagen eis Aidao
psychēi chrēsomenon Thēbaiou Teiresiao·
sentences.l:
‘Mother mine, a need led me down to Hades,
to consult the soul of Theban Tiresias;
sentences.i: ‘Mother, need has brought me down to the house of Hades to consult the soul of Theban Tiresias;
sentences.n: μῆτερ ἐμή is ‘mother mine’. χρειώ is ‘need’, a form of χρεώ. κατήγαγεν is ‘led down’, a plain augmented aorist. εἰς Ἀίδαο has the house understood, as in Attic εἰς ᾅδου; the literal English says ‘to Hades’ and the free English supplies the house. ψυχῇ χρησόμενον is ‘to consult the soul’, a future participle of χράομαι with the dative, the verb used of asking an oracle. Θηβαίου Τειρεσίαο is ‘of Theban Tiresias’, with Τειρεσίαο a genitive in -αο.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πω σχεδὸν ἦλθον Ἀχαιΐδος, οὐδέ πω ἁμῆς
γῆς ἐπέβην, ἀλλ’ αἰὲν ἔχων ἀλάλημαι ὀιζύν,
ἐξ οὗ τὰ πρώτισθ’ ἑπόμην Ἀγαμέμνονι δίῳ
Ἴλιον εἰς ἐύπωλον, ἵνα Τρώεσσι μαχοίμην.
sentences.tr:
ou gar pō schedon ēlthon Achaiïdos, oude pō hamēs
gēs epebēn, all’ aien echōn alalēmai oizyn,
ex hou ta prōtisth’ hepomēn Agamemnoni diōi
Ilion eis eypōlon, hina Trōessi machoimēn.
sentences.l:
for not yet near the Achaean land have I come, nor yet on our
land have I set foot, but ever having misery I wander,
ever since I first followed heavenly Agamemnon
to Ilios of the fine foals, that with the Trojans I might fight.
sentences.i: For I have not yet come near the Achaean land, nor set foot on any land of ours, but I wander always in misery, ever since I first followed heavenly Agamemnon to Ilios of the fine foals, to fight the Trojans.
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ πω is ‘for not yet’. Ἀχαιΐδος is ‘Achaean’ (the land is understood), and ἁμῆς is ‘our’, a Homeric form of ἡμετέρης. γῆς ἐπέβην is ‘set foot on land’; ἐπιβαίνω takes the genitive. αἰὲν ἔχων … ὀιζύν is ‘always having misery’, with ὀιζύς ‘misery’. ἐξ οὗ τὰ πρώτισθ’ is ‘from the time when first’. Ἀγαμέμνονι δίῳ: δῖος is ‘heavenly’, here of a king; Ἴλιον εἰς ἐύπωλον is ‘to Ilios of the fine foals’, a set phrase. μαχοίμην is a purpose optative, ‘that I might fight’. Four lines make one sentence, and the unit keeps them together.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον·
sentences.tr: all’ age moi tode eipe kai atrekeōs katalexon·
sentences.l: But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly;
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, and set it out for me exactly:
sentences.n: The formula of line 140 returns, with the same English. Here it opens a run of three requests to his mother, each built on εἰπέ.

sentences.t: τίς νύ σε κὴρ ἐδάμασσε τανηλεγέος θανάτοιο;
sentences.tr: tis ny se kēr edamasse tanēlegeos thanatoio;
sentences.l: What death-spirit subdued you, of death that lays-at-length?
sentences.i: Which spirit of the death that lays men at length overcame you?
sentences.n: τίς νύ σε κήρ is ‘what death-spirit, then, … you’: κήρ is a power of death, almost a spirit that takes a man. ἐδάμασσε is ‘overcame’, from δαμάζω ‘tame, subdue’. τανηλεγέος θανάτοιο is the epithet translated as ‘that lays men at length’; the meaning of τανηλεγής is not known, and the other ancient guess is ‘bringing long sorrow’. The question is put in general terms; the next unit offers two possible answers.

sentences.t:
ἦ δολιχὴ νοῦσος, ἦ Ἄρτεμις ἰοχέαιρα
οἷς ἀγανοῖς βελέεσσιν ἐποιχομένη κατέπεφνεν;
sentences.tr:
ē dolichē nousos, ē Artemis iocheaira
hois aganois beleessin epoichomenē katepephnen;
sentences.l:
Was it a long sickness, or Artemis, arrow-pourer,
with her gentle shafts assailing, who slew you?
sentences.i: Was it a long sickness, or did Artemis, who showers her arrows, come upon you with her gentle arrows and kill you?
sentences.n: ἦ … ἦ … is ‘either … or …’ in a question. δολιχὴ νοῦσος is ‘a long sickness’. ἰοχέαιρα is ‘who showers her arrows’: the second element is disputed (χέω ‘pour’, or χαίρω ‘delight in’). The second line is a formula for death by a god’s arrows, and its English is the one already fixed for it: οἷς ἀγανοῖς βελέεσσιν ἐποιχομένη κατέπεφνεν is ‘with her gentle arrows coming upon (her prey), killed’.

sentences.t:
εἰπὲ δέ μοι πατρός τε καὶ υἱέος, ὃν κατέλειπον,
ἢ ἔτι πὰρ κείνοισιν ἐμὸν γέρας, ἦέ τις ἤδη
ἀνδρῶν ἄλλος ἔχει, ἐμὲ δ’ οὐκέτι φασὶ νέεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
eipe de moi patros te kai huieos, hon kateleipon,
ē eti par keinoisin emon geras, ēe tis ēdē
andrōn allos echei, eme d’ ouketi phasi neesthai.
sentences.l:
And tell me of my father and my son, whom I left behind,
whether still with them is my prize, or whether some
other of men already holds it, and me no more they say will come home.
sentences.i: And tell me of my father and my son, whom I left behind: whether my prize of honour still stays with them, or some other man already holds it, and they say that I shall come home no more.
sentences.n: πατρός τε καὶ υἱέος are genitives of the persons asked about, ‘of my father and my son’. ὃν κατέλειπον is ‘whom I left’ (the relative is singular and belongs to the son). ἢ ἔτι πὰρ κείνοισιν is ‘whether still with them’, with πάρ for παρά. γέρας is the prize of honour, the privilege of rank that belongs to a man in his own land. ἦέ τις ἤδη ἀνδρῶν ἄλλος ἔχει is ‘or some other of men already holds (it)’. νέεσθαι is the epic infinitive ‘to come, to go home’.

sentences.t:
εἰπὲ δέ μοι μνηστῆς ἀλόχου βουλήν τε νόον τε,
ἠὲ μένει παρὰ παιδὶ καὶ ἔμπεδα πάντα φυλάσσει
ἦ ἤδη μιν ἔγημεν Ἀχαιῶν ὅς τις ἄριστος.
sentences.tr:
eipe de moi mnēstēs alochou boulēn te noon te,
ēe menei para paidi kai empeda panta phylassei
ē ēdē min egēmen Achaiōn hos tis aristos.
sentences.l:
And tell me of my wedded wife’s counsel and mind,
whether she stays by her child and keeps all things steadfast,
or already has married her whoever of the Achaeans is best.’
sentences.i: And tell me of my wedded wife’s counsel and mind: does she stay with her child and keep everything secure, or has the best of the Achaeans already married her?’
sentences.n: μνηστῆς ἀλόχου is ‘wedded wife’: μνηστός is literally ‘wooed’, and a wife won by courtship is a lawfully wedded one. βουλήν τε νόον τε are ‘counsel and mind’, what she plans and what she thinks. ἠὲ … ἦ is ‘whether … or’, and ἔμπεδα means ‘steadfastly, securely’. ἔγημεν is the aorist of γαμέω, said of the man who marries. ὅς τις ἄριστος is ‘whoever is best’. The speech ends at the full stop.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ἡ δ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμείβετο πότνια μήτηρ·
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, hē d’ autik’ ameibeto potnia mētēr·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and she then at once answered, the lady mother:
sentences.i: So I said, and my lady mother answered me at once:
sentences.n: ὣς ἐφάμην is ‘so I spoke’, and ἡ δ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμείβετο is ‘and she at once answered’: ἀμείβετο is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’ without its augment (Attic ἠμείβετο). πότνια is ‘lady’, a title of respect for a woman of standing, here given to a mother. The unit ends at the high dot, and the speech begins next.

sentences.t:
καὶ λίην κείνη γε μένει τετληότι θυμῷ
σοῖσιν ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν·
sentences.tr:
kai liēn keinē ge menei tetlēoti thymōi
soisin eni megaroisin·
sentences.l:
‘Yes, very much, she stays, with enduring heart,
in your halls;
sentences.i: ‘Yes, she stays there, truly, with an enduring heart, in your halls;
sentences.n: His mother answers the last question first. καὶ λίην is ‘yes, very much so’, and κείνη γε ‘she, indeed’. μένει is ‘stays, waits’. τετληότι θυμῷ is ‘with enduring heart’, a dative of manner, from the participle of τλάω. σοῖσιν … μεγάροισιν is a dative plural in -οισιν, ‘in your halls’, with ἐνί placed after its adjective.

sentences.t:
ὀιζυραὶ δέ οἱ αἰεὶ
φθίνουσιν νύκτες τε καὶ ἤματα δάκρυ χεούσῃ.
sentences.tr:
oizyrai de hoi aiei
phthinousin nyktes te kai ēmata dakry cheousēi.
sentences.l:
and sorrowful for her always
waste away the nights and the days, a tear shedding.
sentences.i: and for her the nights and days are always sorrowful, and wear away as she sheds tears.
sentences.n: ὀιζυραί is ‘sorrowful’, from ὀιζύς ‘misery’. οἱ is ‘for her’, the dative of interest. φθίνουσιν is ‘wear away, waste’. δάκρυ χεούσῃ is ‘as she sheds a tear’, a dative feminine participle agreeing with οἱ; the phrase is rendered the same way every time. νύκτες τε καὶ ἤματα is ‘nights and days’, the pair; the Greek puts the nights first.

sentences.t:
σὸν δ’ οὔ πώ τις ἔχει καλὸν γέρας, ἀλλὰ ἕκηλος
Τηλέμαχος τεμένεα νέμεται καὶ δαῖτας ἐίσας
δαίνυται, ἃς ἐπέοικε δικασπόλον ἄνδρ’ ἀλεγύνειν·
sentences.tr:
son d’ ou pō tis echei kalon geras, alla hekēlos
Tēlemachos temenea nemetai kai daitas eisas
dainytai, has epeoike dikaspolon andr’ alegynein·
sentences.i: Nobody yet holds your fine prize of honour. Undisturbed, Telemachus enjoys your domains and the equally shared feasts that it is fitting for a man who dispenses justice to see to;
sentences.n: σὸν δ’ οὔ πώ τις ἔχει is ‘no one yet holds your’. καλὸν γέρας is ‘fine prize’; γέρας is the privilege of rank. ἕκηλος is ‘undisturbed, at ease’. τεμένεα are the lands set apart for a chief, and νέμεται is ‘enjoys, has the use of’. δαῖτας ἐίσας are ‘equal feasts’, each guest having his share. ἐπέοικε is ‘it befits’, and δικασπόλον is ‘who administers justice’ (δίκη ‘justice’ + πολέω ‘busy oneself with’). ἀλεγύνειν is ‘to see to, to arrange’.

sentences.t: πάντες γὰρ καλέουσι.
sentences.tr: pantes gar kaleousi.
sentences.l: for all invite him.
sentences.i: For they all invite him.
sentences.n: The sentence explains the feasts: καλέουσι is the uncontracted ‘they invite’ (Attic καλοῦσι). The object is not stated; it is Telemachus. The full stop falls in the middle of line 187, so the next unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
πατὴρ δὲ σὸς αὐτόθι μίμνει
ἀγρῷ, οὐδὲ πόλινδε κατέρχεται.
sentences.tr:
patēr de sos autothi mimnei
agrōi, oude polinde katerchetai.
sentences.l:
And your father stays there
in the country, and does not go down to the city.
sentences.i: But your father stays right there on his farm, and does not come down to the city.
sentences.n: πατὴρ δὲ σὸς is ‘but your father’; αὐτόθι is ‘right there’, in the country. ἀγρῷ is ‘in the country, on his land’. πόλινδε is ‘to the city’, with the suffix -δε of direction, and κατέρχεται is ‘goes down’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ οἱ εὐναὶ
δέμνια καὶ χλαῖναι καὶ ῥήγεα σιγαλόεντα,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γε χεῖμα μὲν εὕδει ὅθι δμῶες ἐνὶ οἴκῳ,
ἐν κόνι ἄγχι πυρός, κακὰ δὲ χροῒ εἵματα εἷται·
sentences.tr:
oude hoi eunai
demnia kai chlainai kai rhēgea sigaloenta,
all’ ho ge cheima men heudei hothi dmōes eni oikōi,
en koni anchi pyros, kaka de chroï heimata heitai·
sentences.l:
nor has he beds,
bedding and cloaks and glossy rugs,
but he in winter sleeps where the servants are, in the house,
in the dust near the fire, and evil clothes on his skin he wears;
sentences.i: He has no beds, no bedding, cloaks or glossy rugs; in winter he sleeps where the servants sleep, in the house, in the dust near the fire, with poor clothes on his skin;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 188. οὐδέ οἱ εὐναί is ‘nor has he beds’, the dative of possession; δέμνια, χλαῖναι, ῥήγεα are the things a bed is made of: bedding, cloaks, rugs. σιγαλόεντα is ‘glossy’. χεῖμα is an accusative of time, ‘in winter’. ὅθι δμῶες is ‘where the servants (sleep)’. κακὰ … εἵματα is ‘poor garments’, and εἷται is the perfect of ἕννυμι, ‘is clothed’. The sentence runs from the middle of line 188 to the high dot at the end of 191, and the unit keeps it whole.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν ἔλθῃσι θέρος τεθαλυῖά τ’ ὀπώρη,
πάντῃ οἱ κατὰ γουνὸν ἀλωῆς οἰνοπέδοιο
φύλλων κεκλιμένων χθαμαλαὶ βεβλήαται εὐναί.
sentences.tr:
autar epēn elthēisi theros tethaluia t’ opōrē,
pantēi hoi kata gounon alōēs oinopedoio
phyllōn keklimenōn chthamalai beblēatai eunai.
sentences.l:
But when summer comes and flourishing late summer,
everywhere for him, on the rising ground of the vineyard plot,
of fallen leaves low beds are strewn.
sentences.i: But when summer comes, and the flourishing late summer, low beds of fallen leaves are strewn for him everywhere on the rising ground of the vineyard plot.
sentences.n: ἐπὴν ἔλθῃσι is ‘when it comes’, with ἔλθῃσι a subjunctive of ἔρχομαι. τεθαλυῖα ‘flourishing’ goes with ὀπώρη, the late summer when fruit ripens. πάντῃ is ‘everywhere’, and οἱ ‘for him’. κατὰ γουνόν is ‘on the rising ground’, and ἀλωῆς οἰνοπέδοιο is ‘of the vineyard plot’ (οἰνόπεδος: οἶνος ‘wine’ + πέδον ‘ground’). φύλλων κεκλιμένων is ‘of fallen leaves’, lit. ‘leaning, lying down’. βεβλήαται is a perfect passive of βάλλω, ‘have been thrown, strewn’, with the ending -αται for -νται.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ὅ γε κεῖτ’ ἀχέων, μέγα δὲ φρεσὶ πένθος ἀέξει
σὸν νόστον ποθέων, χαλεπὸν δ’ ἐπὶ γῆρας ἱκάνει.
sentences.tr:
enth’ ho ge keit’ acheōn, mega de phresi penthos aexei
son noston potheōn, chalepon d’ epi gēras hikanei.
sentences.l:
There he lies grieving, and great grief in his mind he makes grow,
longing for your homecoming, and harsh old age comes upon him.
sentences.i: There he lies grieving, making great grief grow in his mind as he longs for your homecoming, and harsh old age is coming upon him.
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ ὅ γε is ‘there he’. ἀχέων is ‘grieving’. φρεσὶ πένθος ἀέξει is ‘he makes grief grow in his mind’, ἀέξει being ‘makes grow’. σὸν νόστον ποθέων is ‘longing for your homecoming’. χαλεπὸν δ’ ἐπὶ γῆρας ἱκάνει is ‘harsh old age comes upon (him)’, with tmesis: ἐπὶ … ἱκάνει.

sentences.t: οὕτω γὰρ καὶ ἐγὼν ὀλόμην καὶ πότμον ἐπέσπον·
sentences.tr: houtō gar kai egōn olomēn kai potmon epespon·
sentences.l: for so I too perished, and my doom I met;
sentences.i: For that is how I too perished and met my doom:
sentences.n: οὕτω γάρ is ‘for thus’. ὀλόμην is the unaugmented aorist middle of ὄλλυμι ‘perish’, and πότμον ἐπέσπον is ‘I met my doom’, with ἐπέσπον the aorist of ἐφέπω ‘follow up, encounter’. πότμος is ‘doom, one’s allotted end’. The unit ends at the high dot; four lines follow that say what did not kill her.

sentences.t:
οὔτ’ ἐμέ γ’ ἐν μεγάροισιν ἐύσκοπος ἰοχέαιρα
οἷς ἀγανοῖς βελέεσσιν ἐποιχομένη κατέπεφνεν,
οὔτε τις οὖν μοι νοῦσος ἐπήλυθεν, ἥ τε μάλιστα
τηκεδόνι στυγερῇ μελέων ἐξείλετο θυμόν·
sentences.tr:
out’ eme g’ en megaroisin eyskopos iocheaira
hois aganois beleessin epoichomenē katepephnen,
oute tis oun moi nousos epēlythen, hē te malista
tēkedoni stygerēi meleōn exeileto thymon·
sentences.l:
neither me in my halls the keen-sighted arrow-pourer
with her gentle shafts assailing slew,
nor did any sickness come upon me, such as most of all
with hateful wasting takes the life from the limbs;
sentences.i: It was not the keen-sighted one who showers her arrows who came upon me in my halls with her gentle arrows and killed me, nor did any sickness come upon me, such as most of all takes the life out of the limbs with hateful wasting;
sentences.n: οὔτε … οὔτε … is ‘neither … nor …’. ἐύσκοπος is ‘keen-sighted’, ἰοχέαιρα ‘who showers her arrows’; the pair names Artemis without using her name. Line 199 is a formula already met, with its English: ‘with her gentle arrows … came upon … and killed’. νοῦσος is ‘sickness’. ἥ τε μάλιστα has the epic τε, marking what a sickness generally does. τηκεδόνι στυγερῇ is ‘with hateful wasting’ (τήκω ‘melt’), μελέων ‘from the limbs’ (genitive plural of μέλος), and θυμόν is here the life that leaves the body, rendered ‘life’. Four lines make one sentence, and the unit keeps them together.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά με σός τε πόθος σά τε μήδεα, φαίδιμ’ Ὀδυσσεῦ,
σή τ’ ἀγανοφροσύνη μελιηδέα θυμὸν ἀπηύρα.
sentences.tr:
alla me sos te pothos sa te mēdea, phaidim’ Odysseu,
sē t’ aganophrosynē meliēdea thymon apēura.
sentences.l:
but longing for you and your counsels, glorious Odysseus,
and your gentleness of mind took from me my honey-sweet life.’
sentences.i: No, it was my longing for you, and for your counsels, glorious Odysseus, and your gentleness of mind that took my honey-sweet life away.’
sentences.n: ἀλλά contrasts with the two negatives before. σός τε πόθος is ‘longing for you’: the possessive σός stands for an objective genitive. σά τε μήδεα is ‘your counsels’, what he plans. ἀγανοφροσύνη, ‘gentleness of mind’ (ἀγανός ‘gentle’ + φρήν), is a rare noun. μελιηδέα is the stock ‘honey-sweet’, here of the θυμός, which is again the life. ἀπηύρα is the aorist of ἀπαυράω ‘take away, deprive of’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ γ’ ἔθελον φρεσὶ μερμηρίξας
μητρὸς ἐμῆς ψυχὴν ἑλέειν κατατεθνηυίης.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’, autar egō g’ ethelon phresi mermērixas
mētros emēs psychēn heleein katatethnēuiēs.
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and I, in my mind pondering,
wished the soul of my mother, who had died, to seize.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and I, thinking it over in my mind, wanted to take hold of the soul of my mother, who had died.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ γ’ is ‘so she spoke, and I’. ἔθελον φρεσὶ μερμηρίξας is ‘I wished, having pondered in my mind’, with the aorist participle of μερμηρίζω ‘ponder’. ἑλέειν is the aorist infinitive of αἱρέω, ‘to seize’, with its vowels left open. μητρὸς ἐμῆς ψυχήν … κατατεθνηυίης is the phrase of line 141, the soul of my mother, who had died, given the same English.

sentences.t:
τρὶς μὲν ἐφωρμήθην, ἑλέειν τέ με θυμὸς ἀνώγει,
τρὶς δέ μοι ἐκ χειρῶν σκιῇ εἴκελον ἢ καὶ ὀνείρῳ
ἔπτατ’.
sentences.tr:
tris men ephōrmēthēn, heleein te me thymos anōgei,
tris de moi ek cheirōn skiēi eikelon ē kai oneirōi
eptat’.
sentences.l:
Three times I rushed upon her, and my heart bade me seize her,
and three times from my hands, like a shadow or even a dream,
she flew away.
sentences.i: Three times I rushed toward her, and my heart urged me to take hold of her, and three times she flew from my hands like a shadow or a dream.
sentences.n: τρὶς μέν … τρὶς δέ is ‘three times … and three times’, the old pattern of three tries. ἐφωρμήθην is the aorist passive of ἐφορμάω, ‘I was impelled, rushed’; ἀνώγει is ‘urged’, the imperfect of ἄνωγα. σκιῇ εἴκελον ἢ καὶ ὀνείρῳ is ‘like a shadow or even a dream’, with εἴκελον ‘like’ and a dative of comparison. ἔπτατ’ is ἔπτατο, the aorist of πέτομαι ‘fly’, with the subject (the shade) understood. The full stop falls in the middle of line 208.

sentences.t:
ἐμοὶ δ’ ἄχος ὀξὺ γενέσκετο κηρόθι μᾶλλον,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδων·
sentences.tr:
emoi d’ achos oxy genesketo kērothi mallon,
kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēudōn·
sentences.l:
And to me sharp grief came ever more in my heart,
and speaking to her, winged words I addressed to her:
sentences.i: and sharp grief grew in my heart all the more, and I spoke to her and addressed her with winged words:
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 208. ἐμοὶ δ’ ἄχος ὀξύ is ‘to me sharp grief’, with γενέσκετο, an iterative ‘kept coming to be’, the ending -σκ- marking repetition. κηρόθι μᾶλλον is ‘ever more in the heart’. Line 209 is a formula and keeps its English; line 154 ended with the same words, spoken by his mother (προσηύδα), and now the speaker is Odysseus (προσηύδων, ‘I addressed’). His speech is not in this part.
